Kestrel Retail (Mumbai)

Kestrel Retail runs 600 grocery and fashion stores across India and a growing app business.

Requirements (must have)
- 2+ years of analytics experience
- Strong SQL and one of Python or R
- Experience measuring the impact of campaigns or experiments
- Ability to explain analysis to non-technical stakeholders
Nice to have: retail or banking domain experience

transcript.text: Hi Meera, good to meet you. I'd like to have a first conversation with you about the Business Analyst - Customer Analytics role at Kestrel Retail. It should take about 15 minutes, and there'll be time for your questions at the end. What have you been working on or learning recently in your MBA?
transcript.why: This was a warm-up question to help you settle in. It isn't part of the feedback.

transcript.text: Hi good to meet you too um so in the last few months at IIM Kozhikode I’ve been focusing a lot on analytics as well as marketing actually so apart from my regular coursework like statistics and predictive modeling I took some electives around customer analytics and also retail operations um and in terms of hands-on learning my summer internship at ICICI was quite analytics heavy so I learnt quite a bit about how churn modeling works and how you can actually use behavioral data to spot customers at risk but otherwise at the Analytics Club I’ve been helping juniors with small data hackathons so I got to use tools like Python and Power BI and overall just getting more comfortable at turning large data into something business-relevant yeah so it’s been quite a learning journey and I’m excited about how much of this applies to customer analytics in retail too
Thanks. Walk me through your path from engineering and Mu Sigma to your MBA, including what you’ve focused on since starting it.
transcript.why: I asked about your recent MBA work to understand what you have been focusing on before moving into your broader experience.

transcript.text: yeah sure so I started my undergrad in electronics and communication at PSG College of Technology in Coimbatore and then right after graduation I wanted to work at the intersection of tech and business so that’s how I got into Mu Sigma where I worked for about three and a half years so it was actually my first exposure to analytics at scale because we were solving data problems for large US retailers and I got to work hands-on with forecasting models in R and a lot of SQL and Tableau work too so um after spending a few years with Mu Sigma I took a break due to a personal situation at home I’d prefer not to get into the details but during that time I also picked up some freelance projects mostly for D2C brands who wanted help with their Shopify data and some reporting so I learnt a lot about small business challenges and kind of brushed up my skills with Power BI and cohort analysis and that kept me sharp during my break and after that I felt like it was the right time to formalise my business knowledge and that’s why I came to IIM Kozhikode so since joining the MBA I’ve focused on analytics courses building on my work experience but also picked up marketing and product electives because I wanted a broader view of the retail and consumer space especially how analytics can drive outcomes not just reporting so yeah in summary my journey has been from engineering to hardcore analytics to now developing a more strategic lens through my MBA
What draws you to the Business Analyst - Customer Analytics role at Kestrel Retail, given your decision science experience and recent banking internship?
transcript.why: Your overview covered the main transitions in your path and the work you pursued during your MBA, so I moved to why this role interests you.

transcript.text: so actually I feel like this role at Kestrel Retail is almost like the natural step for me because throughout my professional journey um even at Mu Sigma most of my projects were with retail clients not just in terms of forecasting but also understanding customer-level data and what drives store performance so I realized I really enjoy working with large scale customer and transaction data and getting to the insights that can improve business outcomes and then during my MBA I wanted to get exposure to other domains so that’s why I interned with ICICI Bank but the part that excited me most there was still about understanding customer behavior—like churn risk in savings accounts which is not too different conceptually from customer retention in retail actually and I find the customer analytics space in retail especially interesting because it’s right at the intersection of business impact and analytics—you can directly see how recommendations affect sales, loyalty, merchandising strategies and so on and Kestrel Retail as a company is known for being data-driven and innovative in how it approaches customer experience so I feel like my experience in building forecasting models, automating reports for managers, and doing analytics that connects directly to business decisions would be really useful here um plus I’m genuinely interested in how D2C and omni-channel shifts are changing retail so honestly I feel motivated by both the opportunity to work on new retail analytics problems and the culture of the company
Which part of your work so far most shaped your interest in customer analytics for a retailer like Kestrel?
transcript.why: Your answer linked the role to your retail and banking work, so I asked for the specific part of that experience that led you toward customer analytics.

transcript.text: yeah so I’d say the most impactful experience was actually my main project at Mu Sigma where we built the weekly demand forecasting model for that large US retailer with about eighteen hundred stores so what really shaped my interest in customer analytics was how we had to go beyond just sales numbers and start looking at factors like local events competitor openings promotions everything at store and sometimes even customer segment level so I got to work with granular transaction data and basically had to figure out which patterns affect footfall or basket size and because of that I saw how powerful it is when you can turn raw customer data into something that actually changes store operations or influences how managers think about their categories um also during my freelance stint I worked closely with D2C brands which are much smaller scale but it was hands-on because I could talk to the founders and see directly how repeat rate or cohort behaviour affects their marketing plans so both experiences taught me that customer analytics isn’t just about numbers it’s about influencing product and business decisions and I find that quite motivating because you can see the results much faster in retail so I think that’s why it left an impact and really confirmed my interest in this area
Let’s turn to your ICICI internship. Tell me about the attrition early-warning model you built there.
transcript.why: You connected your interest in customer analytics to work with retail transaction data and D2C brands, so I moved to a specific project from your banking internship.

transcript.text: sure so at ICICI Bank I was part of the retail liabilities analytics team and my summer project was about building an early-warning model to predict which savings account holders were at high risk of closing their accounts within the next ninety days so basically they were seeing a rising trend in attrition especially among newer accounts in two specific regions and wanted to get ahead of it before it affected branch metrics so I started by pulling customer-level transaction data from their data warehouse things like frequency of debit and credit transactions average balance complaints logged, a few digital engagement metrics like app logins and so on and after some feature engineering and variable selection I used logistic regression and a simple gradient boosting classifier in Python to see which features mattered most actually it turned out that sudden drop in digital engagement and any bounce charges in the last month were strong predictors so the final model gave each active account a risk score, and for the top decile cases—like the highest scoring ten percent—they were over four times more likely to close their account than the rest so for the pilot I recommended giving these accounts to the branch managers as a priority callback list and for Chennai and one more region they actually ran this as a pilot and are monitoring results now and overall I got exposed to how large customer datasets are used to drive retention campaigns and how much difference targeting the right segment can make especially in banking where the margins are tight
You compared logistic regression with gradient boosting. Which modeling decision in that process was personally yours?
transcript.why: You described the data and models used, but not which choices were personally yours. I asked about the decisions you made in building the score.

transcript.text: yeah so actually most of the model design and variable selection was my responsibility but I’d say the main decision that was personally mine was to run both logistic regression and gradient boosting in parallel and then sort of compare the explainability and the business interpretability because while gradient boosting was performing slightly better in terms of AUC the stakeholders in the analytics team and especially the business users preferred a more interpretable model for the first rollout so I made the call to use logistic regression results for the actual branch callback list because I could explain very clearly which factors were driving the risk scores and that built more trust with the branch managers who had to act on these lists so I think balancing the slightly higher accuracy of gradient boosting with the practical need for transparency in recommendations—that was a conscious modeling choice from my side also feature engineering, like bucketing digital engagement drops rather than using continuous values, was something I pushed for based on feedback from the business side so yeah those modeling and design choices about what goes live and what stays as a benchmark were mainly mine and something I discussed actively with the analytics lead
You used the top-decile group as the callback list. How was the 4.2x likelihood figure calculated?
transcript.why: You explained which modeling choices were yours, so I asked how the headline 4.2x result was produced and what it was compared against.

transcript.text: yeah so after building the model I scored all the active accounts in the dataset with the final risk score and ranked them from highest to lowest risk so when I mention the top decile that means the top ten percent of accounts with the highest predicted risk score out of the total base and then I looked at the actual attrition rates in the historical data for each decile group so for the top ten percent group I checked what percentage of those accounts actually closed within the ninety-day period in the past and compared that with the average attrition across the full sample so for example let’s say overall attrition in ninety days was like 1.5 percent but for the top decile group it was maybe 6.3 percent so then 6.3 divided by 1.5 roughly gives around 4.2 so that’s how we derived that the high-risk group identified by the model was over four times as likely to attrite in that period compared to the base so it was just a ratio of the event rates between the flagged decile and the overall population and that helped demonstrate to stakeholders that targeting that segment could really improve intervention efficiency
Thanks. Let’s move to campaign impact. Tell me about a time you measured whether an analytics recommendation changed a business outcome.
transcript.why: Your answer explained how the ratio was calculated, but the figures sounded illustrative rather than confirmed results. I’m moving on to hear about another campaign-impact example.

transcript.text: yeah so actually the best example I have is from my freelance work with a D2C skincare brand so basically they were running a lot of discounts every month and felt like they weren’t really getting more loyal customers so I built them a customer cohort dashboard using Shopify export data and Power BI and what we found was that the new customers acquired during heavy discount campaigns were churning much faster like very few of them were making repeat purchases compared to those acquired through content or influencer campaigns so I presented this insight to the founders and recommended that they reduce blanket discount offers and instead target only specific segments based on first purchase date and category so after they changed their campaign strategy for two months to focus more on content-led customer acquisition and segment-specific offers, we tracked repeat purchase rates and overall discount spend and basically their discounting costs dropped by about 15 percent over the next three months and the share of retained customers in new cohorts went up by around 5 percent which they were happy with so I felt like this was a direct impact of the analytics recommendation because we not only changed the campaign approach but also saw measurable change in both spend and retention so that whole feedback loop was quite satisfying for me
